doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Chicago homes, Willard School and getting into DuSable
summary: He lists his addresses, being moved to Burke School to graduate, and using his great-aunt's address to get into DuSable and Captain Dyett's band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah, always. I was born on the west side of Chicago – I forget that address – and moved to 4909 Champlain Avenue on the south side, which is where I was until I was – went to Willard Grammar School [Frances Willard Elementary School], and I stayed there until – I almost graduated from Willard, but my family had moved to 5418 South Parkway [Boulevard], which is [Martin Luther] King Drive now. I kept going to Willard. I used to walk through the park every day. Finally, the principal called me and said, “Listen. You shouldn’t be going here.” He says, “There’s a school right” – it was half a block away from me. I say, “I love Willard.” He said, “We know you do. But you’re going to have go to Burke School.” I said, “How am I going to graduate?” He said, “You can graduate from summer school, so you won’t get behind.” So I went to [Edmund] Burke [Elementary] School in the summer, and they graduated me. Then I went to DuSable.
So you went into DuSable as a freshman there.
You were in the right district to go to DuSable? Or you jimmied the records a little?
No, no. I had to tell some tales again.

Everybody was telling tales, like we used to call them, but they were bare­ faced lies. But we would call them tales, that we lived in the neighborhood, because I did have an aunt that lived across the street, my Aunt Minnie, a relative of – my father’s aunt. She was my great aunt. So I said, “Dad, I got to get into DuSable. I got to get in there.” He said, “You can’t get there, because you don’t live in that vicinity.” I said, “Dad, you got to work it out. Don’t you have somebody somewhere?” Sure enough, he had an aunt living right here. His aunt was right across the street. So I wrote down her address. They all knew I was telling a tale, but they let me in anyway. Because all of us wasn’t in that
district, all of us that were in the band. Everybody wanted to be under Captain Walter Dyett, that great man that taught at DuSable. But that’s way down the line. I must have been 14 by that time.
